title: Will farm animals always suffer? - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Factory farming intensifies along predictable income thresholds (~$1,000 for industrial chicken, ~$10,000 for battery cages, ~$30,000 for warehouse pigs), and the essay argues animal welfare may follow an environmental-Kuznets-style curve that bends only above ~$45,000 average income, and only where cheap substitute technology already exists. The catch: rich-country meat consumption plateaus near 150kg/person rather than falling, and the shift from beef to chicken and farmed fish doubles the number of animals killed per diet even as tonnage declines.

insights.claim: Livestock industrialization follows predictable income thresholds: chicken farming starts to industrialize once a country's average income reaches roughly $1,000, most chickens are in battery cages by $10,000, and virtually all pigs are warehoused above $30,000 average income.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A crude but usable screen for where protein-industrialization capex, feed demand, and animal-welfare regulatory risk arrive next as emerging-market incomes cross each threshold.
insights.quote: Once average incomes reach around $1,000, chicken farming starts to industrialize. By the time a country reaches $10,000, the vast majority of chickens are raised in battery cages.

insights.claim: South Korea's meat supply quintupled between 1961 and 1979 under Park Chung Hee, rose tenfold by 2000, and now exceeds 120 kilograms of meat and seafood per person per year — a compressed template for how fast protein demand scales with industrialization.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The Korean ramp is the base rate for forecasting protein demand curves in currently industrializing economies — a 10x in four decades, not a gradual drift.
insights.locator: Factory farming exists to meet rising demand

insights.claim: Rising meat consumption in poor countries tracks large gains in physical development — South Korean average male height rose from about 160cm in 1961 to about 175cm today, with a similar 165cm-to-175cm gain in Chinese men.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Frames protein demand growth in developing markets as a health-driven secular trend that policy is unlikely to suppress, supporting long-run feed, aquaculture, and animal-protein volumes.

themes.theme: Kuznets curve as the load-bearing analogy

insights.claim: The core analytical question is whether animal suffering behaves like child labor — a harm that declines as societies get richer — or like waste generation, which keeps growing regardless of wealth.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Determines whether alternative-protein and welfare-compliance markets are structural growth stories or perpetual niches; the essay's own evidence leans mixed, not clean.
insights.quote: The question is whether animal suffering is closer to child labor, and will decrease as we grow richer, or to waste generation, meaning animals will continue to suffer in ever-greater numbers.
insights.locator: But Kuznets curves don’t appear in all places

insights.claim: Kuznets curves reliably appear only where the industrial harm has direct local costs to the rich country: London's air pollution halved within a century of Dickens and fell to under a tenth its 1850s dirtiness by 2000, and global forest loss peaked in 1980 and typically reverses at incomes between $5,000 and $15,000.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Harms that are externalized or invisible to affluent consumers — like animal welfare in opaque supply chains — should be expected to bend late or not at all.
insights.locator: The Kuznets curve

insights.claim: Carbon emissions are a counterexample to the Kuznets pattern: they have fallen substantially in Germany and Britain but much less in America and Australia, which remain among the world's biggest emitters despite high incomes.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Wealth alone is a weak predictor of decarbonization or welfare reform — jurisdiction and politics dominate, which argues for country-level rather than income-level positioning on ESG-linked regulatory risk.
insights.quote: Emissions have fallen substantially in Germany and Britain, but much less in America and Australia, which remain some of the world’s biggest carbon emitters.
insights.locator: But Kuznets curves don’t appear in all places

insights.claim: Historical Kuznets curves for sulfur dioxide, particulates, and water pollution were produced by consuming differently rather than consuming less — coal replaced by natural gas for home heating, phosphates removed from detergents — implying the welfare curve may bend through better production methods rather than reduced meat demand.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Points investment attention at welfare-compliant production technology and input substitution rather than at demand destruction narratives for meat.
insights.quote: The way down the curve might not require people to eat less meat, but simply to produce it better.
insights.locator: How we treat farm animals

insights.claim: Rich-country meat consumption tends to plateau rather than fall: Portugal, Spain, the United States, Britain, South Korea, and Australia have all converged on a ceiling near 150 kilograms of meat per person per year, and incomes of $40,000–$50,000 do not reliably trigger a decline.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Implies a hard demand ceiling per capita — global meat volume growth is a population-and-emerging-income story, not a rich-world one, capping downside for incumbents but also capping growth.
insights.quote: The plateauing countries, like Portugal, Spain, the United States, Britain, South Korea, and Australia, have all reached a ceiling of around 150 kilograms of meat per person per year.
insights.locator: But many rich countries aren’t like Germany

insights.claim: About ten European countries including Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, and Denmark have passed peak per-capita meat consumption, with German pork consumption falling over 10 percent in the five years before 2025 and 34 Berlin university cafeterias moving to 96 percent plant-based menus in 2021.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Northern European pork processors and retail meat categories face genuine structural volume decline; institutional foodservice is the fastest-moving channel to watch.
insights.quote: In 2021, 34 cafeterias across Berlin’s universities moved to menus that were 96 percent plant-based.
insights.locator: How much meat do we eat?

insights.claim: Two live dietary trends could break the meat plateau upward: faddish guidelines recommending two grams of protein per kilogram of body weight would require the average American to double meat consumption if half that protein came from meat, and GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic cut total calories but push users toward protein-rich foods.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A non-obvious long for high-protein meat and dairy: GLP-1 adoption may shrink total food volume while raising the meat-and-dairy share of the plate.
insights.locator: Whether this ceiling holds may depend

insights.claim: Eating less meat by weight can mean killing more animals: the average German diet required about ten farmed animals in 1980 but twenty by 2022 — roughly 14 chickens, just under one pig, one sixth of a cow, and six farmed fish — even though Germans ate a fifth less meat.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Tonnage-based ESG and sustainability metrics for protein badly misstate the welfare trend; animal-count metrics invert the conclusion, a live risk for how food companies are scored.
insights.quote: By 2022, even though Germans were eating a fifth less meat, that number had doubled to twenty animals, largely driven by the shift to chicken and farmed fish
insights.locator: More importantly, the kind of animal

insights.claim: Suffering per kilogram varies by orders of magnitude across species — roughly a day or two for beef, dozens of days for chicken, and hundreds or thousands of days for farmed fish — making species mix, not total volume, the dominant welfare variable.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Aquaculture is the least-scrutinized and highest-exposure segment on this metric — the most likely target of the next wave of welfare regulation and campaigning.
insights.quote: Beef implies perhaps a day or two of suffering per kilogram, whereas chicken implies dozens of days of suffering per kilogram and farmed fish hundreds or thousands, depending on the species.

insights.claim: Global welfare improvements are currently being swamped in aggregate: the growth in the number of animals farmed, particularly chickens and fish, outweighs the gains from better treatment everywhere except a handful of countries.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Net-negative aggregate trend means the reform story is a rich-country pocket phenomenon, not a global one — sizing any welfare-linked market off global headlines will overshoot.
insights.quote: The sheer growth in the number of animals consumed, particularly chickens and fish, swamps the gains from better treatment.
insights.locator: Overall, these welfare improvements aren’t enough

insights.claim: New Zealand is the clearest case of a bent curve, having banned battery cages, restricted sow crates, mandated pre-slaughter stunning, and reduced meat eating simultaneously, with Germany, Sweden and a few other wealthy European countries plausibly following.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: These jurisdictions are the leading indicator for welfare regulation that later exports to larger markets via retailer standards and trade rules.
insights.locator: Overall, these welfare improvements aren’t enough

themes.theme: Cheap welfare tech and the cost of production

insights.claim: Decades of single-minded cost optimization have made meat historically cheap — a pound of chicken cost the average American factory worker over half an hour of work in 1946 versus four minutes today — which paradoxically leaves abundant cheap, simple welfare improvements available.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Cheap protein creates slack for welfare upgrades that barely dent unit economics — meaning welfare regulation is far less margin-destructive for producers than commonly assumed.
insights.quote: In 1946, the average American factory worker had to work more than half an hour to buy a pound of chicken. Today it takes four minutes.
insights.locator: For decades, the animal agriculture industry

insights.claim: Cage-free egg conversion has reached 45 percent of American, 62 percent of European, and 82 percent of British hens, at an incremental cost of only one or two cents per egg for two to three times the floor space.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A one-to-two-cent per egg cost delta is trivially passed through — the cage-free transition is a pricing-power opportunity for egg producers, not a cost shock.
insights.quote: Today, 45 percent of American, 62 percent of European, and 82 percent of British hens are kept in cage-free facilities.
insights.locator: In wealthy countries, consumers and companies

insights.claim: Welfare reform arrives through three distinct channels — ballot initiatives in Switzerland, Massachusetts and California, legislation across the European Union, New Zealand and several US states, and pure retailer-and-shopper pressure in Sweden, where almost all hens were cage-free by 2025 without any law.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Retailer-led change can outrun legislation, so monitoring grocery procurement policies gives earlier warning of supply-chain cost shifts than tracking legislatures.
insights.quote: The Swedes didn’t even need legislation. By 2025, almost all hens in Sweden were cage-free thanks to retailers and shoppers rejecting caged eggs.
insights.locator: In some countries and regions, cages

insights.claim: In ovo sexing, which identifies chick sex at the embryo stage so male eggs are discarded rather than day-old male chicks gassed or ground up, has already spared hundreds of millions of chicks in Europe and has only just begun spreading in the US.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: An identifiable technology adoption S-curve with Europe ~10 years ahead of the US — a concrete addressable market for equipment vendors serving American hatcheries.
insights.locator: New technologies can reduce suffering

themes.theme: Why alternative proteins have failed so far

insights.claim: The entire alternative meat industry has yet to exceed 2 percent market share of meat overall, and the author attributes this failure entirely to cost rather than taste, regulation, or consumer resistance.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: If cost is the binding constraint, alt-protein investment theses should be underwritten on unit-cost curves alone; brand and distribution spend before cost parity is wasted capital.
insights.quote: the entire alternative meat industry has yet to reach more than 2 percent market share for meat overall. This is easily explained by costs.

insights.claim: The only cultivated meat on supermarket shelves is a Singaporean product that is just 3 percent cultivated chicken cells and 97 percent plant-based, retailing above twenty dollars per pound — roughly ten times conventional chicken and five times premium pasture-raised.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A 10x price gap on a product that is 97 percent plant filler quantifies how far cultivated meat is from commercial relevance — years of cost-down, not quarters.
insights.quote: a shredded chicken product that is 3 percent cultivated chicken cells and 97 percent plant-based, and retails at more than twenty dollars per pound

insights.claim: Welfare and environmental curves bend only when an undeniable problem coincides with a workable substitute — leaded gasoline levels collapsed within a decade of 1970s phaseouts, while London's air pollution worsened for two centuries before its decline.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Substitute-availability is the timing signal for regulatory inflections: track cost parity, not public sentiment, to time exposure to welfare or substitution-driven regulation.
insights.quote: Those curves began to bend when the problem became undeniable at the same time as a workable substitute existed.

themes.theme: Willingness to pay and the income floor

insights.claim: Belief that farm animals suffer is near-universal and income-invariant — 70 to 90 percent of people from Sudan to Singapore agree — so what actually changes with wealth is willingness to pay, rising from 42 percent of Europe's poorest income quintile to 72 percent of the richest.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Consumer-sentiment surveys on animal welfare carry no predictive signal; only willingness-to-pay data, which tracks income, should inform premium-product sizing.
insights.quote: In European surveys, 42 percent of the poorest quintile say they would pay more for higher-welfare products. Among the richest quintile, it’s 72 percent.
insights.locator: Bending the curve

insights.claim: No poor country has bent the welfare curve — the countries that have sit at average incomes of $45,000 (New Zealand), $55,000 (Germany), and $65,000 (Denmark) — but income is necessary and not sufficient, since Japan, South Korea, and the United States exceed those levels with rising meat consumption and weaker reforms than peers.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Sets a rough $45,000 income floor for welfare-premium markets while flagging that the three largest rich economies are the laggards — the biggest markets are the least likely near-term reformers.
insights.quote: No poor country has bent the curve: New Zealand has an average income of $45,000, Germany $55,000, and Denmark $65,000.
insights.locator: Bending the curve

insights.claim: Animal welfare improves fastest where the enabling technology is already cheap and proven, as stunning machines for chickens and pigs and cage-free housing systems for hens were before scale adoption began.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Screen welfare-tech opportunities on whether the technology is already cost-competitive pre-mandate; those are the ones that scale when regulation arrives.
insights.locator: Animal welfare improves fastest when the technology

insights.claim: The author concludes that even if a Kuznets curve for animal suffering exists, it may take a tremendous amount of time and effort before the other side is visible — an explicitly hedged, low-conviction resolution to the essay's own framing question.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: The author will not underwrite the optimistic case — treat welfare-driven disruption of animal agriculture as a multi-decade thesis, not an investable near-term inflection.
insights.quote: If indeed there is a Kuznets curve for animal suffering, it may take a tremendous amount of time and effort before we see the other side. What we see now is only a glimpse.
